questions.stem: Which of these reactions is not a redox reaction?
options: Iron rusting in moist air to form iron(III) oxide
Zinc displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate
Hydrochloric acid neutralising sodium hydroxide
Methane burning completely in a supply of oxygen
questions.explanation: In HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O no oxidation numbers change; hydrogen ions are transferred, not electrons. Combustion, corrosion and metal displacement all involve electron transfer.

questions.stem: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Which statement about this combustion reaction is correct?
options: Hydrogen is oxidised from +1 to +2, and oxygen is reduced from 0 to -2
No species changes oxidation number, because all the bonds are covalent
Carbon is oxidised from -4 to +4, and oxygen is reduced from 0 to -2
Oxygen is oxidised from 0 to -2, and carbon is reduced from -4 to +4
questions.explanation: Carbon's oxidation number rises from -4 in CH₄ to +4 in CO₂ (oxidation) and oxygen's falls from 0 to -2 (reduction). Hydrogen stays at +1. Covalent reactions can still be redox.

questions.stem: A strip of zinc is placed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. A brown coating forms on the zinc and the blue colour fades. Which pair of half-equations describes this?
options: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → S
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn and Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
Zn + 2e⁻ → Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Zinc atoms lose electrons and dissolve as Zn²⁺, while Cu²⁺ ions gain those electrons and deposit as brown copper, so the blue colour fades. Sulfate is a spectator ion.

questions.stem: When iron rusts, which half-equation shows the reduction reaction?
options: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe
questions.explanation: In rusting, iron is oxidised to Fe²⁺ and dissolved oxygen is reduced to hydroxide ions in the water film. The Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ then react further to form hydrated iron(III) oxide.

questions.stem: Blocks of zinc are bolted to the steel hull of a ship. E°: Zn²⁺/Zn -0.76 V; Fe²⁺/Fe -0.44 V. Why does this protect the steel?
options: Zinc is a stronger oxidising agent, so it removes electrons from the iron
Zinc has the higher E°, so it is reduced in place of the iron in the hull
Zinc forms an oxide coating that spreads to seal the whole of the hull
Zinc is a stronger reducing agent, so it is oxidised in place of the iron
questions.explanation: Zinc's lower E° makes it the stronger reducing agent, so it corrodes and supplies electrons to the iron, which is not oxidised. This is sacrificial protection; the zinc blocks must be replaced as they are used up.

questions.stem: In terms of electrons, what is oxidation?
options: The loss of protons by a chemical species
The sharing of electrons between two atoms
The loss of electrons by a chemical species
The gain of electrons by a chemical species
questions.explanation: Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain; the two always happen together. Loss of protons describes a Brønsted-Lowry acid, not oxidation.

questions.stem: What is an oxidising agent?
options: A species that donates protons and is itself reduced
A species that accepts electrons and is itself reduced
A species that donates electrons and is itself oxidised
A species that accepts electrons and is itself oxidised
questions.explanation: An oxidising agent causes another species to be oxidised by taking its electrons, so the oxidising agent is reduced. A reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is -2, and the total must be zero: 2(+1) + S + 4(-2) = 0, so S = +6. +4 is sulfur's oxidation number in SO₂ or sulfite.

questions.stem: Which half-equation is correctly balanced for the reduction of dichromate ions in acidic solution?
options: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 3e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 7H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6e⁻
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
questions.explanation: Balance Cr, then O with 7 H₂O, then H with 14 H⁺, then charge: the left is +12 before electrons and the right is +6, so 6 electrons are added to the left. Electrons on the right would make it an oxidation.

questions.stem: Aluminium metal reacts with copper(II) ions in solution. Which is the balanced overall equation?
options: 2Al³⁺ + 3Cu → 2Al + 3Cu²⁺
2Al + 3Cu²⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3Cu
Al + Cu²⁺ → Al³⁺ + Cu
3Al + 2Cu²⁺ → 3Al³⁺ + 2Cu
questions.explanation: Each Al loses 3 electrons and each Cu²⁺ gains 2, so 2 Al and 3 Cu²⁺ transfer 6 electrons each way. The equation with single coefficients balances atoms but not charge.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. What happens to the oxygen atoms?
options: All are oxidised from -2 to 0, while the hydrogen atoms are reduced
None change oxidation number, so the reaction is not a redox reaction
Some are oxidised from -1 to 0, and others are reduced from -1 to -2
All are reduced from 0 to -2, while the hydrogen atoms are oxidised
questions.explanation: Oxygen is -1 in H₂O₂. It rises to 0 in O₂ and falls to -2 in H₂O, so the same element is both oxidised and reduced. Hydrogen stays at +1 throughout.

questions.stem: Which element is most likely to act as a reducing agent by losing electrons?
options: Chlorine
Oxygen
Neon
Sodium
questions.explanation: Sodium has one valence electron, which it loses easily to reach a stable full outer shell, so it is a strong reducing agent. Chlorine and oxygen tend to gain electrons, and neon already has a stable shell.

questions.stem: Why do the Group 1 metals become stronger reducing agents going down the group?
options: The atoms become smaller further down, so their valence electrons are pushed out more easily
The valence electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
The nucleus has more protons, so it attracts the valence electron more strongly and releases it
The atoms have more valence electrons further down, so more electrons are available to lose
questions.explanation: Each Group 1 atom has one valence electron, but down the group it sits in a higher shell, further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner electrons. Less energy is needed to remove it, so the metal is more easily oxidised.

questions.stem: Why is fluorine a stronger oxidising agent than iodine?
options: A fluorine atom is smaller, so an added electron is held more strongly by the nucleus
A fluorine atom has fewer valence electrons, so it has more room for extra electrons
An iodine atom has more protons, so it attracts an added electron more strongly
An iodine atom has a full valence shell, so it cannot accept any extra electrons
questions.explanation: Both atoms have seven valence electrons. In fluorine the incoming electron enters a shell close to the nucleus with little shielding, so it is strongly attracted; in iodine the outer shell is far from the nucleus.

questions.stem: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions but not Mg³⁺ ions in its compounds. Why?
options: Magnesium gains one electron after losing three, so its overall charge is +2
Losing two electrons leaves a full outer shell; a third would come from an inner shell
Losing three electrons would leave a full outer shell, but that releases too much energy
Magnesium has only two electrons in total, so it cannot lose a third electron
questions.explanation: Magnesium (2,8,2) loses its two valence electrons to reach the stable 2,8 arrangement. Removing a third electron from the inner shell, close to the nucleus, would need far more energy than is ever recovered.

questions.stem: Standard electrode potentials are measured against which reference half-cell?
options: The standard oxygen half-cell, given a value of 1.00 V
The standard hydrogen half-cell, given a value of 0.00 V
The standard copper half-cell, given a value of 0.00 V
The standard zinc half-cell, given a value of 1.00 V
questions.explanation: Each E° is the potential of a half-cell under standard conditions measured against the standard hydrogen half-cell, H⁺/H₂, defined as 0.00 V. A positive E° means a stronger oxidising agent than H⁺.

questions.stem: E° values: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V; Fe²⁺/Fe -0.44 V; Zn²⁺/Zn -0.76 V. Which species is the strongest reducing agent?
options: Zn(s)
Ag⁺(aq)
Ag(s)
Zn²⁺(aq)
questions.explanation: The strongest reducing agent is on the right of the half-equation with the lowest E°, here zinc metal. Ag⁺ is the strongest oxidising agent, the opposite end of the list.

questions.stem: E°: Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V; Pb²⁺/Pb -0.13 V. What happens when a strip of lead is placed in copper(II) nitrate solution?
options: Lead is reduced to Pb²⁺, and copper ions lose electrons to form copper
Lead is oxidised to Pb²⁺, and copper metal is deposited on the strip
Copper ions are oxidised, and lead metal is deposited from the solution
Nothing happens, because lead has a lower E° than copper has
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ (higher E°) is the stronger oxidising agent and Pb (lower E°) the stronger reducing agent, so Pb + Cu²⁺ → Pb²⁺ + Cu is spontaneous. Forming Pb²⁺ from Pb is oxidation, not reduction.

questions.stem: E°: Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ +0.77 V; I₂/I⁻ +0.54 V. Iron(III) chloride solution is added to colourless potassium iodide solution. What is expected?
options: Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to brown iodine, and Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺
I⁻ oxidises Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, and iodide is reduced to iodine
No reaction occurs, because both E° values are positive
Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺, and iodine is reduced to iodide
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺, in the half-equation with the higher E°, is the stronger oxidising agent and reacts with I⁻: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂. A positive E° on both sides does not stop a reaction; only the relative values matter.

questions.stem: In any electrochemical cell, galvanic or electrolytic, where does oxidation take place?
options: At the anode
At the cathode
In the salt bridge
In the external wire
questions.explanation: Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, in both kinds of cell. Electrons travel through the external circuit from anode to cathode.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is made from Zn/Zn²⁺ and Cu/Cu²⁺ half-cells joined by a potassium nitrate salt bridge. How do the electrons and the nitrate ions move?
options: Electrons flow through the wire to the copper; NO₃⁻ moves into the zinc half-cell
Electrons flow through the wire to the zinc; NO₃⁻ moves into the copper half-cell
Electrons flow through the salt bridge to the copper; NO₃⁻ moves through the wire
Electrons flow through the wire to the copper; NO₃⁻ moves into the copper half-cell
questions.explanation: Zinc is the anode, so electrons leave it through the wire to the copper cathode. Zn²⁺ builds up in the anode half-cell, so anions such as NO₃⁻ move towards it to keep it neutral. Electrons never travel through the salt bridge.

questions.stem: What is the role of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
options: It allows ions to move, keeping each half-cell electrically neutral
It allows electrons to move from one half-cell into the other half-cell
It supplies the reactants that are oxidised and reduced in the cell
It keeps the cell's voltage from rising above a safe working value
questions.explanation: Without a salt bridge, charge would build up in each half-cell and the current would stop. Ions in the bridge move to balance that charge; the electrons move only through the external wire.

questions.stem: A Zn/Cu galvanic cell runs for several hours. What changes are observed?
options: The zinc gets lighter, the copper gets heavier and the blue solution fades
The zinc gets heavier, the copper gets lighter and the blue solution darkens
Both electrodes get lighter, and the blue solution becomes more intense
Neither electrode changes, because only electrons move through the cell
questions.explanation: At the anode zinc dissolves as Zn²⁺, so it loses mass; at the cathode Cu²⁺ ions are reduced and deposit as copper, so the electrode gains mass and the blue Cu²⁺ solution becomes paler.

questions.stem: Which cell diagram represents a galvanic cell in which magnesium is oxidised and silver ions are reduced?
options: Mg(s) | Mg²⁺(aq) || Ag⁺(aq) | Ag(s)
Ag(s) | Ag⁺(aq) || Mg²⁺(aq) | Mg(s)
Mg²⁺(aq) | Mg(s) || Ag(s) | Ag⁺(aq)
Mg(s) | Ag⁺(aq) || Mg²⁺(aq) | Ag(s)
questions.explanation: By convention the anode (oxidation) is written on the left and the cathode on the right, with || for the salt bridge, and each half-cell is written in the order of its reaction: Mg → Mg²⁺ and Ag⁺ → Ag.

questions.stem: A cell is written Ni(s) | Ni²⁺(aq) || Ag⁺(aq) | Ag(s). Which half-equation occurs at the cathode?
options: Ag(s) → Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻
Ni²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Ni(s)
Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s)
Ni(s) → Ni²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: The cathode is on the right of a cell diagram and is where reduction occurs, so silver ions gain electrons. Nickel is oxidised at the anode on the left.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between a galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell?
options: A galvanic cell drives a non-spontaneous reaction; an electrolytic cell uses a spontaneous one
A galvanic cell has no anode or cathode; an electrolytic cell has both electrodes in one beaker
A galvanic cell involves only oxidation; an electrolytic cell involves only reduction
A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous reaction; an electrolytic cell drives a non-spontaneous one
questions.explanation: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. An electrolytic cell uses an external power supply to force a non-spontaneous reaction. Both have an anode and a cathode.

questions.stem: A city bus runs on a hydrogen fuel cell rather than a rechargeable battery. Why does it not need to be plugged in to recharge?
options: Hydrogen and oxygen are supplied continuously, so it runs while fuel is supplied
The fuel cell's electrodes are consumed slowly, so they last the life of the bus
The water produced is split back into hydrogen and oxygen inside the cell itself
The fuel cell generates its own electricity by electrolysing the air around it
questions.explanation: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell whose reactants are fed in from outside and whose product, water, is removed, so it keeps producing electricity as long as fuel arrives. Its electrodes are not consumed.

questions.stem: Why is the platinum catalyst in many fuel cells made as nanoparticles on a carbon support?
options: Nanoparticles raise the cell's standard potential above the difference in E° values
Nanoparticles absorb the water produced, stopping it from flooding the electrodes
Nanoparticles have a large surface area per gram, giving more active sites for less metal
Nanoparticles are oxidised at the anode, supplying extra electrons to the external circuit
questions.explanation: A catalyst works at its surface, and dividing platinum into particles 1 to 100 nm across exposes far more surface for each gram of this expensive metal. The catalyst speeds the electrode reactions without being consumed.

questions.stem: Which statement about a platinum nanoparticle catalyst in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is correct?
options: It speeds up the electrode reactions but does not change the cell's E°
It raises the cell's E° by lowering the activation energy of the reaction
It is used up at the anode, so it must be refilled along with the fuel
It changes the cell's product from water into hydrogen peroxide
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower activation energy, so the electrode reactions are faster and more useful energy is delivered, but the overall reaction and its E° are unchanged. A catalyst is not consumed.

questions.stem: E°: Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V; Zn²⁺/Zn -0.76 V. What is the standard cell potential of a Zn/Cu galvanic cell?
questions.explanation: E°cell = E°(cathode) - E°(anode) = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V. Adding the two values as written gives 0.42 V, which ignores that zinc's half-equation is reversed.

questions.stem: E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V; Ni²⁺/Ni -0.25 V; Mg²⁺/Mg -2.37 V. Which pair of half-cells gives the largest standard cell potential?
options: Copper and silver, 0.46 V
Magnesium and silver, 3.17 V
Magnesium and copper, 2.71 V
Nickel and silver, 1.05 V
questions.explanation: The largest potential comes from the strongest oxidising agent (Ag⁺) paired with the strongest reducing agent (Mg): 0.80 - (-2.37) = 3.17 V. The further apart the two E° values, the larger the cell potential.

questions.stem: E°: Ag⁺/Ag +0.80 V; Zn²⁺/Zn -0.76 V. The cell reaction is Zn + 2Ag⁺ → Zn²⁺ + 2Ag. What is the standard cell potential?
questions.explanation: E°cell = 0.80 - (-0.76) = 1.56 V. Electrode potentials are not multiplied by the coefficients in the equation, so doubling the silver value to get 2.36 V is wrong.

questions.stem: A galvanic cell is made from a metal X in X²⁺(aq) and a standard copper half-cell (Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V). X is the anode and the cell potential is 0.59 V. What is E° for X²⁺/X?
questions.explanation: Copper is the cathode, so 0.59 = 0.34 - E°(X), giving E°(X) = -0.25 V. +0.93 V would make X the cathode, contradicting the information given.

questions.stem: During electrolysis, to which power-supply terminal is the anode connected, and which process occurs at it?
options: The positive terminal; reduction occurs
The negative terminal; reduction occurs
The positive terminal; oxidation occurs
The negative terminal; oxidation occurs
questions.explanation: The positive terminal draws electrons away from the anode, so oxidation happens there. This is the opposite polarity to a galvanic cell, where the anode is negative, but in both the anode is where oxidation occurs.

questions.stem: Inert graphite electrodes are placed in molten sodium chloride and connected to a DC power supply. Which products form?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
Chlorine at the cathode and sodium at the anode
questions.explanation: The melt contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Na⁺ is reduced to sodium at the negative cathode, and Cl⁻ is oxidised to chlorine gas at the positive anode. Hydrogen forms only when water is present.

questions.stem: Copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. E°: S₂O₈²⁻/SO₄²⁻ +2.01 V; O₂,H⁺/H₂O +1.23 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V; H₂O/H₂,OH⁻ -0.83 V. What forms?
options: Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Copper at the cathode and S₂O₈²⁻ at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode and S₂O₈²⁻ at the anode
Copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explanation: At the cathode the strongest oxidising agent present, Cu²⁺ (+0.34 V, above water's -0.83 V), is reduced. At the anode the strongest reducing agent, water (+1.23 V, below sulfate's +2.01 V), is oxidised to oxygen.

questions.stem: A student wants to electroplate a steel key with copper. How should the cell be set up?
options: Key as the cathode and a copper anode, in sodium chloride solution
Key as the anode and a carbon cathode, in copper(II) sulfate solution
Key as the cathode and a copper anode, in copper(II) sulfate solution
Key as the anode and a copper cathode, in copper(II) sulfate solution
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ ions are reduced onto the object being plated, so it must be the cathode, in a solution of copper ions. The copper anode is oxidised, replacing the Cu²⁺ used. With the key as the anode, the steel would corrode.

questions.stem: Aluminium is made by electrolysing aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. Why is an aqueous solution of an aluminium salt not used instead?
options: Water is a stronger oxidising agent than Al³⁺, so hydrogen forms at the cathode
Al³⁺ is a stronger oxidising agent than water, so it reacts with water first
Aluminium salts do not dissolve in water, so no ions are present to carry charge
Water is oxidised at the cathode, so no electrons reach the aluminium ions
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ has a very low E° (-1.66 V), well below that of water, so in aqueous solution water is reduced to hydrogen instead of aluminium being deposited. With no water present in the melt, Al³⁺ is the species reduced.

questions.stem: When a rechargeable battery, such as a lithium-ion cell, is being recharged, what kind of cell is it acting as, and why?
options: A galvanic cell: the spontaneous discharge reaction runs faster while charging
An electrolytic cell: the charger makes the discharge reaction spontaneous
A galvanic cell: the charger supplies extra reactants from outside the cell
An electrolytic cell: the charger drives the non-spontaneous reverse reaction
questions.explanation: During discharge the battery is a galvanic cell. Recharging uses an external power supply to reverse the reaction, regenerating the reactants, which is electrolysis.
